sections.heading: Key points
sections.content:
*   Phone calls are put in place to support the child’s connection with both parents.
*   Parental tension can turn a well-intended phone call into a stressful experience for their child.
*   If required calls consistently cause distress, be open to an adjustment.

**Q:** My son goes back and forth between his mother and me every few days. He’s 4. Although his mother and I don’t agree about much, we miss him when he’s not with us, so we asked for a FaceTime call every night to be added to his custody order. Lately, I’ve noticed that he gets anxious when it’s time to call his mother, and tonight, he said he didn’t want to talk to her. I don’t know what’s going on. What should we do?

**A**: It’s quite common for [parenting](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/parenting "Psychology Today looks at parenting") plans to incorporate a phone or FaceTime call when the child is with the other parent. The idea is that a call will help the child feel close to both parents as they go back and forth between homes.

I’m going to go out on a limb here and say it’s not my favorite approach. Of course, there are times when it works well, particularly with long-distance co-parenting, when the parent and child don’t see each other for weeks or even months at a time. But if the child goes back and forth between parents every few days, strictly scheduled phone calls may interrupt their ability to calmly settle into a routine at their other home.

When I see phone calls become the most disruptive is when the parents are barely talking to each other, and they are required to coordinate a call so the child can touch base with the other parent. This can be especially troublesome when the child is too young to manage the call without help—about your son’s age or younger. These parents must hold the phone and prompt the child to speak, even when they would rather not interact with each other. Some struggle to keep their animosity out of the exchange and have told me they feel the calls are just another way for the other parent to spy on them. When that’s the thinking going into a call, it’s difficult to create a relaxed, positive experience for the child. Simply anticipating the interaction can bring on [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety") for both parents and especially their child.

Based on that, is it really surprising that after a time, the child balks at making phone calls? It can be the same reason some children say they don’t want to go to the other parent’s home. It’s not necessarily what the other parent is doing that prompts the child to say, "No." Sometimes, it’s the tension between the parents, and the child is really saying, “Enough!”

So, do some soul-searching before you demand that a phone or FaceTime call be part of your child's parenting plan. Is the phone call for you or for the child? If the child must check in every day with the other parent, it may not allow them to settle in. Each call can make them revisit their parents’ breakup—every day, with every phone call. The calls can work against the child when the requirement takes priority over how the child is experiencing them.

Now, when parents approach calls cooperatively, a phone call here and there can be a fun way to check in. Send the other parent a pic of gymnastics practice, and the child might initiate a return phone call afterward for some positive reinforcement. Or, if the child requests to speak to the other parent, that’s a cue to help make the connection. When you hear your child's voice, a soothing response might be, “Hey, buddy! It’s great to hear your voice!” Not, “Oh my gosh, I miss you so much. Life just isn’t the same when you’re not here.” Although you might truly feel that way, sharing those feelings can add to his anxiety. He may feel caught between the two people he loves the most: “Mom (or Dad) misses me, and I can’t be there.” Think of the pressure this puts on a child.

sections.heading: Tips to Make FaceTime Calls Go More Smoothly
sections.content:
The success of intermittent phone calls depends largely on how parents manage them. If you are determined to incorporate calls into the parenting plan, consider these tips to help them go more smoothly:

*   Don’t play games or look for ways to prevent your child from connecting with their other parent.
*   Honor scheduled call times, while allowing reasonable flexibility when your child’s activities or needs require it.
*   Find a comfortable place for calls, but there’s no need to exile your child to a back room. Normalize the interaction. Aim for a positive atmosphere with enough privacy for your child to feel at ease.
*   Don’t turn calls into a bone of contention. Remember, your child did not choose to live in two homes, and coordinating calls is not their responsibility.
*   If your child asks to speak to the other parent during your parenting time, help make that happen.
*   Check your attitude when it’s time for a call. Your child can pick up on your negativity, which can make transitions harder and interfere with their ability to settle in.
*   Keep calls appropriate to your child’s age and [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") span. A 4-year-old may want to show you a toy, say goodnight, and get back to playing. A short call can still be a good call.
*   Take an interest without conducting an interview. “What was fun today?” invites conversation. Questions about the other parent’s activities or visitors put your child in the middle.
*   Keep adult business between adults. A call with your child is not the time to discuss schedules, money, or disagreements with the other parent.
*   Give your child permission to enjoy the other home. “Have fun with Mom!” or “Enjoy your evening with Dad!” lets your child know that being happy there is okay.
*   End warmly, without [guilt](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/guilt "Psychology Today looks at guilt"). “I loved talking with you. See you Saturday!” offers reassurance without making your child responsible for how much you miss them.
*   If calls consistently upset your child, take that seriously. Discuss the pattern with the other parent at a separate time, away from your child, and focus on what would make the contact more comfortable.

THE BASICS

*   [What's a Parent's Role?](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/parenting)
*   [Take our Authoritative Parenting Test](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/tests/personality/parenting-style-test)
*   [Find a family therapist near me](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/therapists?category=parenting)

If a call is required, it’s up to the parents to make it a positive experience for their child. If they consistently struggle to do that, it’s time to seek a change to the arrangement rather than keep putting the child through a [stressful](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/stress "Psychology Today looks at stressful") exchange. The purpose of the call is to support the child’s relationship with both parents, and that purpose should guide how the adults handle it.

Phone calls can be a great way to touch base if the parents handle the interaction collaboratively. If they reach out to one another, reinforcing each other’s place in their child’s life, then a phone or FaceTime call is a great way to ensure continuity and predictability. But if a phone call is put in place to establish territory or out of insecurity—“I’m afraid he might forget about me”—it can leave the child trying to soothe a parent’s anxiety rather than receiving help managing his own.

items: Don’t play games or look for ways to prevent your child from connecting with their other parent.
Honor scheduled call times, while allowing reasonable flexibility when your child’s activities or needs require it.

Find a comfortable place for calls, but there’s no need to exile your child to a back room. Normalize the interaction. Aim for a positive atmosphere with enough privacy for your child to feel at ease.
Don’t turn calls into a bone of contention. Remember, your child did not choose to live in two homes, and coordinating calls is not their responsibility.
If your child asks to speak to the other parent during your parenting time, help make that happen.
Check your attitude when it’s time for a call. Your child can pick up on your negativity, which can make transitions harder and interfere with their ability to settle in.

Keep calls appropriate to your child’s age and [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") span. A 4-year-old may want to show you a toy, say goodnight, and get back to playing. A short call can still be a good call.
Take an interest without conducting an interview. “What was fun today?” invites conversation. Questions about the other parent’s activities or visitors put your child in the middle.
Keep adult business between adults. A call with your child is not the time to discuss schedules, money, or disagreements with the other parent.
Give your child permission to enjoy the other home. “Have fun with Mom!” or “Enjoy your evening with Dad!” lets your child know that being happy there is okay.

End warmly, without [guilt](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/guilt "Psychology Today looks at guilt"). “I loved talking with you. See you Saturday!” offers reassurance without making your child responsible for how much you miss them.

If calls consistently upset your child, take that seriously. Discuss the pattern with the other parent at a separate time, away from your child, and focus on what would make the contact more comfortable.

# Are FaceTime Calls to the Other Parent Always a Good Idea?

## Consider your child's experience when planning co-parenting communication.

### Key points

*   Phone calls are put in place to support the child’s connection with both parents.
*   Parental tension can turn a well-intended phone call into a stressful experience for their child.
*   If required calls consistently cause distress, be open to an adjustment.

**Q:** My son goes back and forth between his mother and me every few days. He’s 4. Although his mother and I don’t agree about much, we miss him when he’s not with us, so we asked for a FaceTime call every night to be added to his custody order. Lately, I’ve noticed that he gets anxious when it’s time to call his mother, and tonight, he said he didn’t want to talk to her. I don’t know what’s going on. What should we do?

**A**: It’s quite common for [parenting](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/parenting "Psychology Today looks at parenting") plans to incorporate a phone or FaceTime call when the child is with the other parent. The idea is that a call will help the child feel close to both parents as they go back and forth between homes.

I’m going to go out on a limb here and say it’s not my favorite approach. Of course, there are times when it works well, particularly with long-distance co-parenting, when the parent and child don’t see each other for weeks or even months at a time. But if the child goes back and forth between parents every few days, strictly scheduled phone calls may interrupt their ability to calmly settle into a routine at their other home.

When I see phone calls become the most disruptive is when the parents are barely talking to each other, and they are required to coordinate a call so the child can touch base with the other parent. This can be especially troublesome when the child is too young to manage the call without help—about your son’s age or younger. These parents must hold the phone and prompt the child to speak, even when they would rather not interact with each other. Some struggle to keep their animosity out of the exchange and have told me they feel the calls are just another way for the other parent to spy on them. When that’s the thinking going into a call, it’s difficult to create a relaxed, positive experience for the child. Simply anticipating the interaction can bring on [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety") for both parents and especially their child.

Based on that, is it really surprising that after a time, the child balks at making phone calls? It can be the same reason some children say they don’t want to go to the other parent’s home. It’s not necessarily what the other parent is doing that prompts the child to say, "No." Sometimes, it’s the tension between the parents, and the child is really saying, “Enough!”

So, do some soul-searching before you demand that a phone or FaceTime call be part of your child's parenting plan. Is the phone call for you or for the child? If the child must check in every day with the other parent, it may not allow them to settle in. Each call can make them revisit their parents’ breakup—every day, with every phone call. The calls can work against the child when the requirement takes priority over how the child is experiencing them.

Now, when parents approach calls cooperatively, a phone call here and there can be a fun way to check in. Send the other parent a pic of gymnastics practice, and the child might initiate a return phone call afterward for some positive reinforcement. Or, if the child requests to speak to the other parent, that’s a cue to help make the connection. When you hear your child's voice, a soothing response might be, “Hey, buddy! It’s great to hear your voice!” Not, “Oh my gosh, I miss you so much. Life just isn’t the same when you’re not here.” Although you might truly feel that way, sharing those feelings can add to his anxiety. He may feel caught between the two people he loves the most: “Mom (or Dad) misses me, and I can’t be there.” Think of the pressure this puts on a child.

## Tips to Make FaceTime Calls Go More Smoothly

The success of intermittent phone calls depends largely on how parents manage them. If you are determined to incorporate calls into the parenting plan, consider these tips to help them go more smoothly:

*   Don’t play games or look for ways to prevent your child from connecting with their other parent.
*   Honor scheduled call times, while allowing reasonable flexibility when your child’s activities or needs require it.
*   Find a comfortable place for calls, but there’s no need to exile your child to a back room. Normalize the interaction. Aim for a positive atmosphere with enough privacy for your child to feel at ease.
*   Don’t turn calls into a bone of contention. Remember, your child did not choose to live in two homes, and coordinating calls is not their responsibility.
*   If your child asks to speak to the other parent during your parenting time, help make that happen.
*   Check your attitude when it’s time for a call. Your child can pick up on your negativity, which can make transitions harder and interfere with their ability to settle in.
*   Keep calls appropriate to your child’s age and [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") span. A 4-year-old may want to show you a toy, say goodnight, and get back to playing. A short call can still be a good call.
*   Take an interest without conducting an interview. “What was fun today?” invites conversation. Questions about the other parent’s activities or visitors put your child in the middle.
*   Keep adult business between adults. A call with your child is not the time to discuss schedules, money, or disagreements with the other parent.
*   Give your child permission to enjoy the other home. “Have fun with Mom!” or “Enjoy your evening with Dad!” lets your child know that being happy there is okay.
*   End warmly, without [guilt](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/guilt "Psychology Today looks at guilt"). “I loved talking with you. See you Saturday!” offers reassurance without making your child responsible for how much you miss them.
*   If calls consistently upset your child, take that seriously. Discuss the pattern with the other parent at a separate time, away from your child, and focus on what would make the contact more comfortable.

If a call is required, it’s up to the parents to make it a positive experience for their child. If they consistently struggle to do that, it’s time to seek a change to the arrangement rather than keep putting the child through a [stressful](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/stress "Psychology Today looks at stressful") exchange. The purpose of the call is to support the child’s relationship with both parents, and that purpose should guide how the adults handle it.

Phone calls can be a great way to touch base if the parents handle the interaction collaboratively. If they reach out to one another, reinforcing each other’s place in their child’s life, then a phone or FaceTime call is a great way to ensure continuity and predictability. But if a phone call is put in place to establish territory or out of insecurity—“I’m afraid he might forget about me”—it can leave the child trying to soothe a parent’s anxiety rather than receiving help managing his own.
